title: Butterfly Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: per-cell left-wing/right-wing/gap checks versus measuring each row by its distance from the nearest tip and building both wings directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a butterfly shape with 2n minus 1 rows, where every row has two wings of stars, one on the left and one on the right, growing toward each other until they meet at the widest row, then shrinking apart again.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Butterfly Opening and Closing Its Wings
blocks.text: Picture a butterfly at the moment its two wings meet fully open, flat against each other with no gap left between them, and then imagine that same butterfly gradually closing its wings both above and below that moment, leaving a growing gap between the two wingtips the further a row is from that middle point.

blocks.caption: Two wings of stars grow toward each other, meeting at the widest row

blocks.text: With n = 1, the two wings collapse into a single touching star.
No rows at all, so nothing is printed.

The diamond already showed that measuring a row's distance from the nearer tip collapses a widen-then-narrow shape into a single formula. It is worth checking exactly what changes and what stays the same when a row is split into two separate wings instead of one block.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The same distance-from-nearest-tip value, m equal to min of r and 2n minus r, still correctly describes how far along the shape any given row is, exactly as with the diamond.

Observation 2: The genuine difference here is what that distance controls, in the diamond it set a single growing star region with a leading gap, here it instead sets the size of two separate wings, one on each side, with the gap sitting between them instead of in front of them.

Observation 3: Testing a small example, n equal to 4, shows that every single row is exactly 2n characters wide, no matter how large or small its wings are, only the split between stars and gap changes, never the total.

Observation 4: Since m already gives the size of each wing directly, the gap size follows immediately as whatever is left over, 2 times n minus m, and all three pieces, left wing, gap, right wing, can be built directly and concatenated.
Checking that the total row width never changes is a simple but powerful self check, if any built row comes out a different length than 2n, something in the wing or gap formula is wrong.

For every row, first work out its distance from the nearer tip, then check every one of the 2n columns individually, deciding whether that position falls inside the left wing, the right wing, or the gap between them.

items: Loop over every row r, from 1 to 2n minus 1.
Compute m, the distance of this row from whichever tip is closer.
Check every one of the 2n columns for this row.
Print a star if the column is inside the first m positions, the left wing.
Print a star if the column is inside the last m positions, the right wing.
Otherwise print a space, the gap between the two wings.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, then check left wing, right wing, or gap

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: m is computed once per row exactly as with the diamond, folding both the widening and narrowing halves into one shared distance value.
The inner loop always runs the same fixed 2n times per row, reflecting that the total row width never changes across the whole shape.
Each of the 2n columns is checked individually against both the left wing and right wing boundary, even though those boundaries only ever change at two specific positions per row.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column in every row is checked against both wing conditions before deciding what to print.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since every row checks a fixed 2n columns and there are proportional to n such rows.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: once the wing size m and the gap size for a row are known, checking every column individually adds nothing, since only the boundary positions of the two wings ever change, everything in between them is always the same character. Both wings and the gap can instead be built directly, in three single operations.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: once m is known, checking whether each of the 2n columns belongs to the left wing, the right wing, or the gap repeats a decision that only ever changes at two fixed boundary positions.

What stays the same as the diamond: the underlying insight, m equal to min of r and 2n minus r, still measures every row's progress through the shape in one shared value.

What is different here: instead of one growing star region with a leading gap, there are now two independently sized wings with the gap sitting between them, and the total row width, 2n, stays fixed the entire time.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, three repeat operations, one for the left wing, one for the gap, one for the right wing, build the entire row in three steps instead of 2n individual checks.

The core idea: compute m once per row, then build the left wing, the gap, and the right wing directly, and concatenate all three.

For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, then build the left wing, the gap, and the right wing directly, each with a single operation, and concatenate all three into one row string. This removes all per cell branching, needing only one print call per row.
For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, then build both wings and the gap between them directly, and print the whole row with a single call.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, build both wings and the gap directly

codes.python:
def butterfly_pattern(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top tip to bottom tip
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        gap = 2 * (n - m)
        row = "*" * m + " " * gap + "*" * m         # build both wings and the gap directly
        print(row)                               # one print call per row instead of per character


if __name__ == "__main__":
    butterfly_pattern(4)

blocks.text: This works because m, exactly as with the diamond, correctly measures every row's distance from the nearer tip, and because the total row width is always fixed at 2n, the gap size follows immediately as whatever remains after both wings are accounted for, 2 times n minus m; a direct repeat operation constructs each wing in one step, and another constructs the gap, with no dependence on checking individual columns.

items: m is computed once per row as the minimum of r and 2n minus r, exactly the same distance measurement already used for the diamond.
A direct repeat operation builds the left wing as m stars, another builds the gap as 2 times n minus m spaces, and a third builds the right wing as m more stars.
Concatenating those three pieces and printing once per row completes the entire butterfly without ever checking an individual column.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own m value, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all 2n minus 1 rows with newline characters assembles the complete butterfly as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole shape, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: A butterfly shares the exact same distance from the nearest tip idea used for the diamond, the only real difference is what each row is built from, two growing wings with a shrinking gap between them, instead of a single growing block of stars with a leading gap.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how is this related to the diamond", think: it reuses the same distance-from-nearest-tip measurement, but splits the row into two wings and a gap instead of one block and a leading gap.
If the interviewer says "does every row have the same total width", think: yes, always 2n, verify any built row against that as a sanity check.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell wing checks in the brute force version, two wings and a gap built per row in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing that reuses the diamond's distance-from-nearest-tip measurement, but splits each row into two independent, mirrored wings around a shrinking central gap instead of a single growing block with a leading gap.

Core Idea: compute m, a row's distance from the nearer tip, exactly as with the diamond, then build a left wing of m stars, a gap of 2n minus 2m spaces, and a right wing of m stars, all three pieces built directly and concatenated.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: a fixed total row width is a strong invariant, verifying it holds for every row is a fast way to catch a wrong wing or gap formula.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape with two nested loops; explaining the fixed-width invariant and the shared distance measurement is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: m equals min of r and 2n minus r, then build wing, gap, wing, of sizes m, 2n minus 2m, m.
